meaning: Says the situation is urgent: this is no time to be doing something, because something more important needs doing.
connection: Verb ている form + 場合じゃない／場合ではない

senses.label: This is no time to ...
senses.meaning: Now is not the time to be doing this. It implies there is something more urgent to do. It often sounds impatient, like you're pushing yourself or urging someone else.
senses.connection: Verb ている form + 場合じゃない (casual)／場合ではない (written, formal); in speech also 「〜てる場合じゃない」
examples: This is no time to be sleeping. Let's hurry up and get ready.
This is no time to cry. Let's go to the hospital right away.
The exam is only three days away. This is no time to be playing around.

senses.label: Rhetorical question / scolding
senses.meaning: The rhetorical form 「〜ている場合か」 is even stronger, like “Is this really the time to be ...?” It is mostly used to scold someone or to push yourself.
senses.connection: Verb ている form + 場合か／場合ですか
examples: Is this really the time to be playing games?!
Is this something to laugh about? This is going to turn into a big problem.

notes: The preceding verb is normally in the ている／てる form, referring to what is going on right now or what someone is stuck doing: ✕「今は寝る場合じゃない」→ ○「今は寝ている場合じゃない」.
This phrase amounts to accusing the listener of “doing something pointless.” Saying 「〜ている場合じゃないですよ」 to a superior or client is very rude; use a softer line such as 「まずは〜を優先したほうがよろしいかと思います」.
The rhetorical 「〜ている場合か！」 is a scolding and sounds harsh. Use it only with close friends or to rev yourself up; with outsiders it is basically picking a fight.

The first part is something the speaker considers pointless or not urgent right now. If the act itself should never be done (illegal, against the rules), use 「〜てはいけない」 or 「〜べきではない」 instead of this pattern.

daily.title: Pushing yourself before a deadline
daily.description: Talking to yourself when an assignment is due soon but you're still on your phone.
daily.example: This is no time to be looking at my phone. I have to write my report.

daily.title: A friend in an emergency
daily.description: Your friend is panicking, and you tell them to calm down and act.
daily.example: This is no time to be feeling down. Let's try calling first.

daily.title: A parent hurrying a child
daily.description: The child is dawdling and about to be late, so the parent hurries them.
daily.example: This is no time to be eating so slowly. It's already eight o'clock!

work.title: Speaking up in a meeting
work.description: With sales falling, the manager urges everyone to act now.
work.example: This is no time to wait and see what other companies do. Let's take action right away.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator criticizes the government for not acting.
work.example: The government can't afford to just keep debating.

etymology: 「場合」 originally means “situation” or “occasion”. 「〜ている場合ではない」 literally means “this is not a situation for doing ...”, which came to mean “you shouldn't be doing ... now”.

similar.title: 〜どころではない
similar.explanation: 「〜どころではない」 usually follows a noun or the dictionary form and means “there is no way I can think about ...” for objective reasons (「忙しくて旅行どころではない」). 「〜ている場合じゃない」 stresses the speaker's judgment that “you shouldn't be doing this now,” often urging someone on or scolding oneself.

similar.title: 〜てはいられない
similar.explanation: 「〜てはいられない」 means “I can't go on (idly) ...”; the point is that the speaker can't sit still and must act (「のんびりしてはいられない」). 「〜ている場合じゃない」 stresses that the timing is wrong, and it can be used to urge other people.

similar.title: 〜てばかりはいられない
similar.explanation: 「〜てばかりはいられない」 means “I can't keep on ... forever,” mostly about a continuing negative state (「泣いてばかりはいられない」), and sounds gentler. 「〜ている場合じゃない」 is more urgent: stop right now.

similar.title: 〜場合は
similar.explanation: Same source: both use the noun 「場合」 (situation, occasion). 「〜場合は」 is neutral, “in the case of ...,” and is used to state rules; 「〜ている場合じゃない」 denies that occasion: “now is not the time for ....”

formation: It is built from 「ている」 (an ongoing action or state), the formal noun 「場合」 (situation, occasion) and 「じゃない」 (casual 「ではない」). Literally: “this is not the kind of moment in which one is doing ...”. Here 「場合」 means the present situation, and denying it says “the current situation does not allow this state to continue”; hence “now is no time for ..., you should be doing something more important.” 「ている」 is used because the target is something happening right now or something one may be sinking into. Replace 「じゃない」 with the rhetorical 「か」 and you make the listener admit “this is not the time,” which is why it turns into a scolding.

meaning: Someone only does one thing and fails to do what they should, or something has just one (negative) quality. Usually expresses dissatisfaction or criticism.
connection: Noun／Verb dictionary form or te-form／Adjective + ばかりで、〜 (negative result or evaluation)

senses.label: Only does ..., never does ...
senses.meaning: Someone only does one thing and doesn't do what they should, like “all they do is ..., and they never ...”. The second part is usually negative and shows the speaker's frustration.
senses.connection: Noun／Verb dictionary form + ばかりで; Verb te-form + ばかりで (keeps doing ...). Common: 「口ばかりで」, 「文句を言うばかりで」
examples: He's all talk and never does anything.
My little brother just plays games and doesn't study at all.
Everyone just complains, and nobody helps.

senses.label: Just ..., nothing good
senses.meaning: Something has only one quality and nothing else to recommend it, like “it's just ..., and not even ...”. Mostly used for negative evaluations.
senses.connection: i-adjective dictionary form／na-adjective + な + ばかりで; Noun + ばかりで
examples: This movie is just long. It isn't interesting at all.
That restaurant was just expensive. The food was nothing special.
There were just too many people, so we couldn't take our time looking around.

notes: 「〜たばかりで」 means “has just ..., so ...” (「入社したばかりで、まだ分からない」); it is about time and has nothing to do with “nothing but.” With the た form it is not this grammar point.
One extra 「なく」 changes the meaning: 「〜ばかりでなく」 means “not only ... but also ...,” adding information with no complaint. ✕ Don't read 「口ばかりでなく」 as “all talk, no action.”
This pattern carries clear criticism and dissatisfaction. Saying 「〜さんは口ばかりで…」 to a superior or client is very rude; in formal situations, describe others neutrally, e.g. with 「〜にとどまっている」.
Connection: nouns attach directly (「口ばかりで」), な-adjectives need 「な」 (「便利なばかりで」), and verbs take the dictionary form or て-form (「言うばかりで」「遊んでばかりで」).

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A mother complains that her child is always on their phone.
daily.example: My kid just looks at his phone all day and never plays outside.

daily.title: Reviewing a restaurant
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend about a trendy restaurant.
daily.example: That place is just famous. The food wasn't all that great, was it?

work.title: Criticizing a meeting
work.description: Coworkers privately complain about an unproductive meeting.
work.example: The meeting was just long, and nothing got decided.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentary says a policy is nothing but slogans.
work.example: The plan only sets goals and lacks concrete measures.

etymology: 「ばかり」 comes from 「はかり」, the stem of the verb 「計る（はかる）」 (to measure). It first meant “amount, extent”, then “about” and “only”. Adding 「で」 (state or reason) gives “only ..., and so ...”.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: Same source and similar meaning: 「〜てばかりいる」 goes at the end of a sentence to describe “doing nothing but ...” (「ゲームをしてばかりいる」). 「〜ばかりで」 goes mid-sentence and is followed by what was not done or by a negative result.

similar.title: 〜ばかり (nothing but)
similar.explanation: Same source: 「〜ばかり」 (nothing but) means “all, nothing but ...” (「甘い物ばかり食べる」) and is a neutral limiter. 「〜ばかりで」 adds 「で」 to lead into a second part, stressing “only this, without what should be there,” with a note of dissatisfaction.

similar.title: 〜ばかりに
similar.explanation: Same source: 「〜ばかりに」 means “just because ... (a bad result followed)” and the result is regrettable (「嘘をついたばかりに信用を失った」). 「〜ばかりで」 means “only ..., not ...,” and the second part is usually something that should be there but isn't.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: Same source: 「〜ばかりでなく」 means “not only ... but also ...,” adding items with no critical tone. 「〜ばかりで」 is followed by a negative or critical remark: “all ... and no ...”.

formation: It combines the limiting particle 「ばかり」 (only, nothing but) with 「で」 (the continuative form of 「だ」, a pause or listing). 「ばかり」 restricts the scope to the first item: “this and nothing else.” 「で」 pauses the sentence and leads into the second part. The result reads “only X (while Y ...)”, where Y is something that should be there but isn't, or a negative evaluation. Because it focuses on what is missing, this pattern naturally carries the speaker's dissatisfaction and criticism.

meaning: A softer version of 「〜てみなさい」. Adults say it to children, or seniors to juniors: “Try ...”, “Go ahead and ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + ごらん（なさい）

senses.label: Try doing ...
senses.meaning: Encourages someone to try something, like “go on, try ...”. Warm and kind. Usually said by parents or teachers to children or juniors.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + ごらん／ごらんなさい. Common: 「やってごらん」, 「食べてごらん」, 「言ってごらん」
examples: It's delicious. Try a bite.
It's not scary. Try doing it yourself.
Tell me what happened.

senses.label: Look / Think about it
senses.meaning: Draws someone's attention to something, or guides them to think, like “look at ...” or “think about ...”. Often used with 「ほら」 or 「よく」.
senses.connection: 「見る」, 「考える」, 「思い出す」, etc. + てごらん
examples: Look up at the sky! There's a rainbow.
Think carefully about how the other person feels.

senses.label: Just try it (warning)
senses.meaning: 「〜てごらんなさい」 can be a warning: “Just try ... and see what happens.” It is usually followed by a bad outcome.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + ごらん（なさい）、〜よ
examples: Go ahead and say that to the teacher. You'll definitely get scolded.

notes: Today 「〜てごらん」 is spoken from higher to lower (parent to child, teacher to student). Saying 「見てごらん」 to a superior or client is very rude: ✕「部長、この資料を見てごらんください」→ ○「部長、この資料をご覧ください」.
It can't be used about yourself: ✕「私も食べてごらん」→ ○「私も食べてみる」. 「〜てごらん」 is only for urging the listener.

When 「〜てごらんなさい」 is used as a warning it is ironic, meaning “go ahead and try ... (and see what happens)”: 「もう一度言ってごらんなさい」 = say that one more time, I dare you! It doesn't really invite the listener to do it.
Although it contains 「ご覧」, 「〜てごらん」 is not honorific. To a senior, say “please try ...” with 「〜てみてください」.

daily.title: Teaching a child to ride a bike
daily.description: A parent encourages the child to try pedaling.
daily.example: Daddy's holding on, so try pedaling.

daily.title: A walk with a child
daily.description: A mother points out flowers by the road.
daily.example: Look over there! Pretty flowers are blooming.

daily.title: A teacher guiding a student
daily.description: A student gives a wrong answer, and the teacher asks them to think again.
daily.example: Think about it carefully one more time.

work.title: A senior coaching a new employee
work.description: A friendly senior tells a new employee to try it on their own first.
work.example: First, try writing the proposal yourself. I'll look it over later.

etymology: 「ごらん」 is written 「ご覧」 and is short for 「ご覧になる」／「ご覧なさい」, honorific forms of 「見る」. It was originally a respectful way to refer to someone's “looking”. Combined with the “try” sense of 「〜てみる」, it became a gentle version of 「〜てみなさい」.

similar.title: 〜てみる
similar.explanation: Same source and similar meaning: 「ごらん」 and 「みる」 both mean “look.” 「〜てみる」 means “try doing” and can be used about yourself (「食べてみる」); 「〜てごらん」 is only for urging others, is equivalent to 「〜てみなさい」, and can only be used to inferiors.

similar.title: 〜なさい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜てごらん」 is short for 「〜てご覧なさい」, so like 「〜なさい」 it is an imperative and can only be used to those below you. 「〜なさい」 is a general instruction, “do ...”; 「〜てごらん」 means “try doing ...” and sounds friendlier.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜てください」 is a polite request usable with anyone; to politely say “please try ...” use 「〜てみてください」. 「〜てごらん」 is friendly but condescending and can't be used with superiors.

formation: It is the te-form of a verb + 「ごらん」. 「ごらん」 is short for 「ご覧なさい」: 「ご」 (honorific prefix) + 「覧」 (look) + 「なさい」 (imperative of 「なさる」), originally “please look.” The structure runs parallel to 「〜てみる」: the 「みる」 there is also “look,” so “do it and see” → “try doing.” Swap that “look” for the honorific imperative 「ご覧なさい」 and you get 「〜てみなさい」 in a gentler guise. Since the core is still an imperative, it can be used only toward those below you; the honorific element just makes it sound friendlier. The warning use is sarcasm: “go on, try it (and see what happens).”

meaning: Describes your own action humbly, as if you were doing it with the other person's permission. Extremely common in business.
connection: Causative te-form + いただく (Group 1 verbs: 〜せていただく; Group 2 verbs, 来る, する: 〜させていただく)

senses.label: Humbly stating your action
senses.meaning: Means “allow me to ...”. You present your action as something the listener has permitted. Very humble. Common in speeches, announcements, and formal remarks.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + いただきます. Common: 「説明させていただきます」, 「休ませていただきます」, 「発表させていただきます」
examples: Well then, let me begin the meeting.
I will be taking tomorrow off because I'm not feeling well.
Allow me to briefly introduce myself.

senses.label: Asking permission
senses.meaning: 「〜させていただけませんか」 and 「〜させていただけますか」 politely ask to be allowed to do something. More polite than 「〜させてください」.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + いただけませんか／いただけないでしょうか／いただきたい
examples: Would you mind if I made a copy of this document?
I'd like some time to think about that matter.

senses.label: Being given the chance
senses.meaning: In the past tense, it expresses thanks for having been given the chance to do something, like “I had the privilege of ...”.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + いただきました／いただいて
examples: It was a valuable experience for me.
Thank you for the wonderful time yesterday.

notes: Godan verbs take 「〜せていただく」: ✕「読まさせていただく」「行かさせていただく」→ ○「読ませていただく」「行かせていただく」. Adding an extra 「さ」 (sa-ire kotoba) is a common error and sounds non-standard.
Don't mix up who does the action: 「休ませていただけませんか」 asks to let “me” rest, while 「休んでいただけませんか」 asks “you” to rest. The meanings are completely different.

Use it only for things that need the other person's permission or that benefit from their favor. Using it for things unrelated to them (「A大学を卒業させていただきました」) or several times in one breath sounds long-winded and overly polite, and some people dislike it; just say 「卒業しました」 or 「〜いたします」.
The 「見せる」 in 「見せていただく」 means “show,” so 「見せていただけますか」 means “could you show me?” For “may I look?” use 「拝見してもよろしいでしょうか」.

daily.title: Wedding speech
daily.description: A friend gives a speech on behalf of the guests at a wedding.
daily.example: As a friend of the groom, allow me to say a few words.

daily.title: A sign at a shop
daily.description: A closure notice posted at a store entrance.
daily.example: We are closed today due to circumstances.

work.title: Presenting to a client
work.description: A salesperson starts presenting a product to a client.
work.example: Now, allow me to explain our new product.

work.title: Replying to an email
work.description: Humbly confirming something in a reply to a client.
work.example: I have checked the contents.

work.title: Asking for more time
work.description: Asking your boss for time to think something over.
work.example: Could I take that matter back with me and look into it?

etymology: It combines the causative 「〜させる」 (let someone do) with 「いただく」 (humbly receive). Literally: “I receive from you the favor of letting me do ...”. Framing your action as a kindness from the listener expresses humility.

similar.title: 〜させてください・〜させてもらう
similar.explanation: Same source and similar meaning: both are built on the causative. 「〜させてください」 directly asks for permission; 「〜させてもらう」 is for peers. 「〜させていただく」 is the most deferential, used mostly in formal and business settings.

similar.title: 参る・申す・いたす (special humble verbs)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「説明いたします」 uses the humble verb 「いたす」 to say humbly what you do, concise and proper. 「〜させていただく」 adds “with your permission,” which is more polite but wordy if overused.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Same source: both use 「いただく」. 「〜ていただけませんか」 asks the other person to do something; 「〜させていただけませんか」 asks the other person to let you do something, so the actor differs.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Same source: 「〜ていただく」 means “I receive the favor of your doing ...,” the action being theirs; 「〜させていただく」 adds the causative 「させ」, so the action becomes mine: “I receive your permission to do ....”

formation: It consists of the causative 「（さ）せる」 (make/let someone do), 「て」 and 「いただく」 (humble form of 「もらう」, to receive). 「〜させてもらう」 means “receive from the other person the favor of being allowed to do,” and replacing 「もらう」 with 「いただく」 makes it humble. In this structure the actor is “I,” while the permission comes from the other person, so my own action is dressed up as a favor granted by them, which sounds extremely deferential. Because the structure presupposes “the other person's permission,” using it for things unrelated to them sounds unnatural, which is the source of complaints about overuse. Godan verbs take 「せ」 and the others 「させ」, simply following the ordinary causative rules.

meaning: 「〜て済む」 means a matter can be settled just by doing this. 「〜ずに済む」 means you got by without having to do something.
connection: Verb te-form／Noun + で + 済む; Verb ない-stem + ずに済む, or Verb ない-form + で済む

senses.label: ... is all it takes
senses.meaning: A problem is settled in a lighter way or at a smaller cost, like “it only took ...” or “got off with ...”. Often carries relief that it wasn't worse. The negative 「〜て済む問題ではない」 means “this isn't something you can fix just by ...”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + 済む; Noun + で済む. Common: 「軽い怪我で済んだ」, 「謝って済む問題じゃない」
examples: I was in an accident, but I got off with only minor injuries.
One phone call can take care of it, so you don't need to come all the way here.
This isn't something you can fix just by apologizing.

senses.label: Get by without ...
senses.meaning: Something you might have had to do turned out to be unnecessary, like “be spared from ...” or “not have to ...”. Usually expresses relief.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + ずに済む (する→せずに済む)／Verb ない-form + で済む
examples: My friend lent me one, so I didn't have to buy an umbrella.
It was caught early, so I didn't need surgery.
I could reach them by email, so I didn't have to go into the office.

senses.label: Avoiding a bad outcome
senses.meaning: Luckily, something unwanted didn't happen: “fortunately didn't ...”. The verb before it is usually something negative like 「けがをする」, 「大事になる」 or 「遅れる」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずに済んだ／ないで済んだ (often with 「おかげで」 or 「早めに」)
examples: Thanks to noticing it early, it didn't turn into anything serious.
I was wearing a seatbelt, so I didn't get hurt.

senses.label: Managing without
senses.meaning: 「〜ずに済ませる／〜ないで済ませる」 means finding a way to get by without doing something. It implies active arrangement.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ずに済ませる／ないで済ませる
examples: If possible, I'd like to get through this without surgery.
I skipped lunch.

notes: A one-word difference reverses the meaning: 「〜ずに済む」 = it got settled without doing (relief); 「〜ずにはすまない」 = it won't be settled without doing (must do). 「謝らずに済んだ」 means “I didn't have to apologize,” while 「謝らずにはすまない」 means “I have to apologize.”
「する」 becomes 「せずに」: ✕「しずに済む」→ ○「心配せずに済む」.

The “thank goodness it was only ...” relief fits only your own situation. Saying 「軽い怪我で済んでよかったですね」 or 「これで済みますよね」 to the person who suffered sounds like you are belittling their loss, and is very rude.
「名詞＋で済む」 means “it was settled with only this much cost”: 「軽いけがで済んだ」 is “got off with only a minor injury,” while 「けがをせずに済んだ」 is “wasn't injured at all”; the degree differs.
The transitive 「〜ずに済ませる」 means actively managing not to do something; telling a client 「確認せずに済ませました」 sounds like cutting corners, so use it carefully at work.

daily.title: Relieved it was cheap
daily.description: Telling a friend your phone repair didn't cost much.
daily.example: The repair only cost 3,000 yen.

daily.title: Getting a ride
daily.description: A friend drives you home, so you don't need other transport.
daily.example: Thanks to you giving me a ride, I didn't have to take a taxi.

daily.title: A parent scolding a child
daily.description: The child just wants to say sorry and be done with it.
daily.example: If saying sorry fixed everything, we wouldn't need the police.

daily.title: At the doctor
daily.description: Telling your family it wasn't serious and you won't be hospitalized.
daily.example: It was just a mild cold, so I didn't have to stay in the hospital.

work.title: Reporting how a problem was handled
work.description: Telling your boss that a problem was solved quickly.
work.example: Because we dealt with it early, it didn't turn into a big problem.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting that earthquake damage was limited.
work.example: Fortunately, no one was injured.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Explaining that acting early avoided losses.
work.example: Because we responded early, we avoided a major loss.

etymology: 「済む」 originally means “(a matter) ends, is settled”. It is generally thought to share a root with 「澄む」 (to become clear), from the image of things settling down. 「〜て済む」 is “settled with ...”, and 「〜ずに済む」 is “settled without doing ...”.
formation: 「〜て済む」 consists of the te-form of a verb (or a noun + 「で」, expressing means or method) + 「済む」 (to be settled, to be finished); literally, “it ends up settled by doing it that way.” Because it stresses “it ended with only this much cost,” it naturally gives a sense of “small cost, thankfully not worse”; the negative 「〜て済む問題ではない」 means “it is not a problem that can be settled with ...”. 「〜ずに済む」 consists of 「ずに」 (classical negative 「ず」 + 「に」, “in a state of not doing”) + 「済む」: “things were settled without doing ...” → “be spared from ..., not have to ...,” which is why it often carries relief.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜なくてもいい」 just says “it's fine not to do it,” which is permission, and can be said to others. 「〜ずに済む」 stresses “you might have had to, but in the end you didn't,” with a sense of relief, and mostly describes results.

similar.title: 〜ずにはすまない／〜ないではすまない
similar.explanation: Same source: also built on 「済む」, but 「〜ずにはすまない」 means “it won't be settled unless you ...; must ...,” the opposite of 「〜ずに済む」. They differ by just 「は」, so keep them apart.

similar.title: 〜てすみません
similar.explanation: Same source: the apologetic 「すみません」 is the negative of 「済む」, 「済みません」, originally “(if this goes on) my conscience isn't settled.” 「〜て済む」 uses the affirmative sense of 「済む」, “to be settled.”

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: 「〜ことはない」 means “there's no need to ...,” mostly in comforting or advising the listener (「心配することはない」); 「〜ずに済む」 states that some circumstance spared you from doing something.

meaning: Casual forms of 「〜てはだめ」 and 「〜てはいけない」. Expresses prohibition: “you mustn't ...”, “don't ...”.
connection: Verb te-form (て→ちゃ, で→じゃ) + だめ／いけない

senses.label: Prohibition
senses.meaning: Says something is not allowed. Direct. Mostly used by parents to children, or between people who are close.
senses.connection: Verb te-form: 〜て→〜ちゃ, 〜で→〜じゃ + だめ／いけない／いけません. E.g. 「触っちゃだめ」, 「飲んじゃだめ」
examples: You can't play here.
Don't push that button.
If you've been drinking, you mustn't drive.

senses.label: Warning / telling yourself
senses.meaning: Says you shouldn't do something, or reminds yourself not to, like “you can't ...”. Often used to encourage someone or yourself.
senses.connection: Verb te-form (ちゃ／じゃ) + だめだ／いけない
examples: I can't give up now.
You shouldn't say bad things about people.

notes: One 「な」 changes the meaning to its opposite: 「食べちゃだめ」 = don't eat it; 「食べなくちゃだめ」 = you must eat it.
Verbs whose te-form ends in 「で」 change to 「じゃ」: ✕「飲んちゃだめ」→ ○「飲んじゃだめ」「遊んじゃだめ」.
The tone is blunt and used with children and close friends. Saying 「触っちゃだめですよ」 to a superior or client is rude; say 「恐れ入りますが、お手を触れないでください」 or 「〜はご遠慮ください」.
「ちゃ」 also appears in 「〜ちゃう」「〜ちゃった」 (contractions of 「てしまう」): 「食べちゃった」 = I ate it up, which has nothing to do with prohibition, so don't confuse them.

daily.title: A mother warning her child
daily.description: The child reaches for a hot pan, and the mother stops them.
daily.example: It's hot, don't touch it!

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A friend just went through a breakup, and you tell them not to lose heart.
daily.example: You can't let one failure get you down.

daily.title: Watching anime
daily.description: A line where characters warn each other.
daily.example: Didn't they tell you not to open this door?

work.title: A senior advising a new employee
work.description: A friendly senior quietly gives a new employee a tip.
work.example: You shouldn't be on your phone in front of customers.

etymology: 「ちゃ」 is a sound change of 「ては」 (te wa → cha), and 「じゃ」 of 「では」 (de wa → ja). 「だめ」 was originally written 「駄目」, a point in the game of Go that is useless to both players. It came to mean “no good, not allowed”.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Same source and meaning: 「〜ちゃだめ・〜ちゃいけない」 are the casual contractions of 「〜てはいけない」. 「〜てはいけない」 can be used in writing and more formal situations, and sounds a bit more formal than 「〜ちゃだめ」.

similar.title: 〜ないでください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ないでください」 is a polite request, “please don't ...,” usable with strangers. 「〜ちゃだめ」 is a direct prohibition, usable only with children or close friends.

similar.title: 〜てはならない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning and same source: 「〜てはならない」 is also “must not ...,” but is very formal, found in regulations and admonitions (「法律に違反してはならない」). 「〜ちゃだめ」 is the most colloquial form.

similar.title: 〜ては・〜では (bad consequence)
similar.explanation: Same source: 「〜ては」 means “if you keep ..., (a bad result follows)” (「そんなに食べては太るよ」). 「〜ちゃだめ」 is 「ては」 + 「だめ」, directly judging that result as “no good.”

formation: It consists of the te-form of a verb + 「は」 (marks a condition or topic) + 「だめ／いけない」 (no good); literally “if you do ..., it's no good.” In speech 「ては」 contracts to 「ちゃ」 and 「では」 to 「じゃ」. 「だめ」 was written 「駄目」, originally a point in Go that is useless to both players, extended to “no good, useless.” The structure is “condition + negative verdict”: put an action into the condition and label it “no good,” and you get a prohibition; said to yourself, it is a self-warning. 「〜なくちゃいけない」 has exactly the same structure, except that the first part has the negative 「なく」 (“it's no good if you don't”), so it means “must.”

meaning: Used with a negative to say strongly “never” or “absolutely not”. Also used to deny something firmly but politely: “by no means ...”.
connection: 決して + Verb ない-form／negative adjective／〜ではない

senses.label: Never ...
senses.meaning: Expresses a strong denial or determination, like “never” or “will never”. Serious in tone and more formal than 「絶対に〜ない」.
senses.connection: 決して + Verb ない-form／〜ません. Common: 「決して忘れない」, 「決して諦めない」
examples: I will never forget your kindness.
No matter how hard it gets, I will never give up.
He is someone who never lies.

senses.label: Strictly prohibited
senses.meaning: 「決して〜ないでください」 and 「決して〜てはいけない」 express a strict prohibition or strong warning. Common in safety notes and manuals.
senses.connection: 決して + 〜ないでください／〜てはいけません
examples: It is dangerous, so never touch it.
You must never tell anyone about this.

senses.label: By no means ...
senses.meaning: 「決して〜ではない」 and 「決して〜わけではない」 deny someone's view in a measured way, like “by no means ...” or “it's not at all that ...”.
senses.connection: 決して + Noun・Adjective + ではない／わけではない; 決して + negative adjective
examples: This problem is by no means easy.
It's not at all that I'm against his opinion.

notes: It must be matched with a negative: ✕「決して行きます」→ ○「決して行きません」. To emphasize an affirmative, use 「必ず」 or 「絶対に」.
Don't confuse total and partial negation: 「決して正しくない」 = definitely not right; 「必ずしも正しくない」 = not necessarily right. Mixing them up changes the meaning a lot.
「決して〜ないでください」 is very stern and common on warning signs and in manuals. Said to a customer's face it sounds like an order; soften it to 「〜なさらないようお願いいたします」.
「決して悪くない」 and 「決して安くはない」 are often understatements: the first really means “quite good,” the second “pretty expensive.” Don't take them only literally.

daily.title: Making a promise to a friend
daily.description: A friend tells you a secret, and you solemnly promise.
daily.example: Don't worry, I'll never tell anyone about this.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character makes a firm resolution.
daily.example: I will probably never forget that day.

work.title: Warning in a manual
work.description: A warning in an appliance manual.
work.example: Never open the cover while the power is on.

work.title: A speech of determination
work.description: A leader expresses determination in a speech.
work.example: We will do our best never to betray your expectations.

etymology: 「決して」 is the te-form of the verb 「決する」 (to decide) used as an adverb. It originally meant “having made up one's mind”. It later came to be used only with negatives, meaning “not ... under any circumstances”.

similar.title: まったく〜ない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「まったく〜ない」 means “not at all,” focusing on degree and describing objectively (「まったく知らない」). 「決して〜ない」 focuses on will and assertion, and is often used for resolve or prohibition.

similar.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「全然〜ない」 is common in speech and means “not at all” in degree (「全然分からない」). 「決して〜ない」 is more formal and written, mostly for resolve or strong denial.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「ちっとも〜ない」 is colloquial “not in the least,” often with a complaint (「ちっとも来ない」). 「決して〜ない」 is for solemn resolve or prohibition, not for complaining.

similar.title: 必ずしも〜ない・必ずしも〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Often compared: 「必ずしも〜ない」 is partial negation, “not necessarily ...”; 「決して〜ない」 is total negation, “never ....” Their strength of meaning is completely different.

formation: 「決して」 is the te-form of the verb 「決する」 (to decide, settle) used as an adverb, originally “resolutely, with firm resolve.” It modifies the negation that follows and fixes it in place, giving “resolutely not ...” → “never ...”. Since 「決して」 itself only asserts, it gets meaning from the negative that follows, so in modern Japanese it is fixed in agreement with negation. Modifying 「〜ないでください」 or 「〜てはいけない」 it fixes the prohibition → strictly forbidden; modifying 「〜ではない」 or 「〜わけではない」 it fixes the denial of some view → “by no means ...”.

meaning: Used with a negative to mean “not particularly” or “not really”. 「別に」 on its own means “Nothing” or “Not really”.
connection: 別に + Verb ない-form／negative adjective／〜ではない

senses.label: Not particularly ...
senses.meaning: Says there's nothing special worth mentioning, like “not really” or “not particularly”. Often used to play something down or to show you don't mind.
senses.connection: 別に + 〜ない／〜ません／〜わけではない
examples: I'm not angry or anything.
I don't have any particular plans today.
It's not like I dislike him.

senses.label: No need to ...
senses.meaning: 「別に〜なくてもいい」 means “there's no particular need to ...”. Relaxed tone.
senses.connection: 別に + 〜なくてもいい／〜なくてもかまわない
examples: There's no need to hurry.
It doesn't have to be today.

senses.label: As a one-word answer
senses.meaning: 「別に。」 on its own means “Nothing” or “Whatever”. It sounds cold and can come across as annoyed or rude.
senses.connection: On its own: 別に。／別に……
examples: “What's wrong?” “Nothing.”

notes: Answering with just 「別に。」 sounds cold and impatient. Never say it to a superior, client or elder; say 「いえ、特に何もありません」 instead.
In business, “no problem” is 「特に問題ありません」. 「別に問題ありません」 may carry a dismissive “what's the big deal?” tone.
「別にいいけど」 literally means “it's fine,” but it often carries reluctance or dissatisfaction, so it isn't a sincere “no problem.”
Without a negative, 「別に」 means “separately, in addition”: 「送料は別にかかります」 = shipping is charged separately, not “nothing in particular.”

daily.title: A friend asks if you mind
daily.description: A friend worries you're upset, and you say it's fine.
daily.example: I don't really mind, so it's okay.

daily.title: Asked what you want
daily.description: Your family asks what you want for your birthday.
daily.example: There's nothing I particularly want.

daily.title: Watching a Japanese drama
daily.description: A rebellious teenager answers a parent coldly.
daily.example: “How was school?” “Whatever.”

work.title: Telling someone there's no rush
work.description: A coworker says the documents will be late, and you say it's not urgent.
work.example: It's not urgent, so next week is fine.

etymology: 「別」 means “separate, different”, and 「別に」 originally meant “separately, especially”. With a negative it came to mean “nothing in particular”, and it became the set phrase “not really”.

similar.title: 〜あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「あまり〜ない」 shows degree, “not very ...” (「あまり好きではない」). 「別に〜ない」 means “not particularly ...,” often with an “I don't mind, no need” tone.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜わけではない」 is partial negation, “it's not that ...”. It is often combined as 「別に〜わけではない」, which softens it further and sounds gentler.

similar.title: 決して〜ない
similar.explanation: Often compared: also an adverb matched with a negative. 「決して〜ない」 is strong denial, “never”; 「別に〜ない」 is casual and merely plays things down.

similar.title: 〜は別として
similar.explanation: Same source: both are built on 「別」 (another, a distinction). 「〜は別として」 means “setting ... aside,” putting something “to one side”; 「別に〜ない」 means “there is nothing separate or special.”

formation: It is the noun 「別」 (another, a distinction) + 「に」 (making it adverbial); 「別に」 originally means “separately, specially (differently from the usual).” Matched with a negative, what is denied is “anything separate or special,” giving “nothing in particular ...” → “not really ...”. Since only the “special” part is denied, the tone is toned down rather than emphatic, and often carries a sense of “I don't mind, no need.” Saying just 「別に。」 drops the negative and leaves only “nothing special,” which is why it can sound cold.

meaning: Used with a negative potential form and similar expressions to mean “there's no way I can ...” or “simply cannot ...”.
connection: とても + negative potential form／〜できない／〜とは思えない

senses.label: Simply can't
senses.meaning: No matter how hard you try, it's impossible, like “there's no way ...” or “simply can't ...”. Usually followed by a negative potential form.
senses.connection: とても + Verb potential form in the negative (食べられない, 読めない)／できない／無理だ
examples: There's no way I can eat this much food by myself.
Finishing this job in one day is completely impossible.
I could never afford a car that expensive.

senses.label: Hard to believe
senses.meaning: 「とても〜とは思えない」 and 「とても〜には見えない」 mean “I can hardly believe ...” or “doesn't look ... at all”. Often expresses surprise, admiration, or doubt.
senses.connection: とても + 〜とは思えない／〜には見えない
examples: She doesn't look sixty at all.
I can hardly believe that's a true story.

notes: 「とても」 with an affirmative means “very,” but with the negative of a potential form it means “absolutely cannot”: 「とても食べられない」 = I simply can't eat it, not “very much can't.”
To say “not very ...” use 「あまり〜ない」: ✕「この店はとても高くない」→ ○「この店はあまり高くない」.
Refusing with 「とても無理です」 is a flat refusal. To customers or superiors, soften it with something like 「少々難しいかと存じます」.
「とても〜には見えない」 can be a compliment (「とても六十歳には見えない」) or an insult (「とても社長には見えない」 = doesn't look like a company president at all); saying the latter to the person concerned is very rude.

daily.title: Turning down a challenge
daily.description: A friend invites you to run a full marathon, but you think it's impossible.
daily.example: A full marathon? There's no way I could run that.

daily.title: Complimenting someone
daily.description: Meeting a friend's mother and being surprised at how young she looks.
daily.example: Your mom doesn't look like she's in her fifties at all.

work.title: Explaining a schedule to your boss
work.description: Explaining that the deadline is too tight to meet.
work.example: With this few people, there's no way we'll make it by the end of the month.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting serious disaster damage.
work.example: The damage is severe, and recovery in just a few days will be impossible.

etymology: 「とても」 is generally thought to come from 「とてもかくても」 (“whatever one does”). It originally meant “in any case”, and with a negative meant “not ... no matter what”. Later it also came to mean “very” in positive sentences, which is its most common use today.

similar.title: 〜っこない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜っこない」 also means “no way,” (「勝てっこない」) but is very colloquial and casual. 「とても〜ない」 works in speech and writing and sounds more composed.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ようがない」 means “there is no way to ...,” stressing that no means can be found (「連絡しようがない」). 「とても〜ない」 stresses that ability or conditions fall far short.

similar.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「全然〜ない」 means “not at all ...,” not limited to ability (「全然知らない」). 「とても〜ない」 is used only when “you can't, in ability or conditions.”

similar.title: なかなか〜ない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「なかなか〜ない」 means “not easily ..., not for a long time,” implying that with time it might be done. 「とても〜ない」 means “by no means possible.”

formation: 「とても」 is generally thought to derive from 「とてもかくても」 (whether this way or that), originally “in any case.” Combined with the negative of the potential, it means “by no means can it be done,” and this pattern preserves that old sense. The emphatic “by all means ...” was later transferred to affirmative sentences, giving the most common modern meaning, “very.” So look at what follows: with negatives such as “can't, unable, doesn't look like,” take it as “by no means ...”; with an ordinary positive evaluation, it is “very.”

meaning: Expresses a guess the speaker isn't confident about: “maybe”, “possibly”. Often paired with 「かもしれない」.
connection: もしかしたら／もしかすると + 〜かもしれない; もしかして + question

senses.label: Maybe ...
senses.meaning: Something is possible, but the speaker isn't sure, like “maybe” or “perhaps”. The sentence often ends with 「かもしれない」 or 「のではないか」.
senses.connection: もしかしたら／もしかすると + plain form + かもしれない. 「もしかすると」 is slightly more formal
examples: It might rain tomorrow.
Perhaps he has already gone home.
We might not make it in time.

senses.label: Could it be ...?
senses.meaning: 「もしかして」 with a question shows you've suddenly realized a possibility and want to check, like “Could it be ...?” or “Don't tell me ...”. Very common in speech.
senses.connection: もしかして + 〜ですか／〜の？／〜じゃない？
examples: Are you Mr. Tanaka, by any chance?
Are you mad at me?

notes: It needs to be matched with an expression of possibility: ✕「もしかしたら明日は雨だ」→ ○「もしかしたら明日は雨かもしれない」.
Don't confuse it with the hypothetical 「もし〜たら」: ✕「もしかしたら雨が降ったら中止です」→ ○「もし雨が降ったら中止です」. 「もしかしたら」 is speculation, “maybe,” not “if.”
It signals low certainty. Using 「もしかしたら」 for something you are sure about may make people think you are unsure, which matters especially in work reports.
「もしかして、〜？」 is very casual. To confirm the identity of a client you are meeting for the first time, 「失礼ですが、〜様でいらっしゃいますか」 is more appropriate.

daily.title: Waiting for a friend
daily.description: Your friend is late, and you guess why.
daily.example: Maybe he got lost.

daily.title: Running into someone
daily.description: You see someone who looks familiar and check if it's them.
daily.example: Hey, aren't you Yamada?

daily.title: Can't find something
daily.description: You can't find your keys and guess where you left them.
daily.example: Maybe I left them at the office.

work.title: Warning your boss about a delay
work.description: Letting your boss know in advance that a delivery may be late.
work.example: The delivery might be one day late.

etymology: Made of 「もし」 (if) + 「か」 (question) + 「したら／すると」 (conditional), literally “if it should be so”. 「もしかして」 is the te-form version and is mostly used in speech to check something.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning and often used together: 「〜かもしれない」 goes at the end to express possibility; 「もしかしたら」 goes at the start to announce that an uncertain guess follows. 「かもしれない」 alone also works.

similar.title: 〜だろう
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜だろう」 is a more confident guess (“probably”). 「もしかしたら」 expresses a smaller chance (“maybe”), so the degrees of certainty differ.

similar.title: もしも〜たら
similar.explanation: Same source: both contain 「もし」 (if). 「もしも〜たら」 is a hypothetical condition, “if ...”; 「もしかしたら」 is not a hypothesis but speculation, “maybe.”

formation: It consists of 「もし」 (if, supposing) + the question particle 「か」 + 「したら／すると」 (the conditional of 「する」); literally, “if (there is such a possibility) ...”. 「もし」 introduces a supposition, 「か」 adds uncertainty, and 「したら」 frames the whole as “in the case where it holds,” so what follows is presented as a speculation with low probability. Since it is only a preview at the start, the end of the sentence needs a possibility expression such as 「かもしれない」 to match. 「もしかして」 is the te-form, ending on “supposing that ...,” fitting a possibility that suddenly occurs to you and that you check with the listener right away.

meaning: Uses a rhetorical question to gently express a guess or opinion: “Isn't it ...?”, “I think maybe ...”.
connection: Plain form (na-adjective・Noun + な) + のではないか／んじゃないか／んじゃない？

senses.label: Soft guess
senses.meaning: States the speaker's guess or opinion without asserting it, like “isn't it ...?” or “I think maybe ...”. Softer than saying it outright.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではないか／のではないでしょうか (polite)／んじゃない？ (casual)
examples: Isn't this plan a bit unrealistic?
Doesn't he already know?
Wouldn't this color suit you better?

senses.label: Worry / anxiety
senses.meaning: 「〜のではないかと思う／心配する」 expresses worry that something bad might happen, like “I'm afraid ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではないかと + 心配だ／不安だ／思う
examples: I was so worried I might fail the exam that I couldn't sleep.
I thought the trains might stop because of the rain, so I left early.

senses.label: Gentle suggestion
senses.meaning: Phrases like 「〜たほうがいいんじゃない？」 make a suggestion softly, without pushing.
senses.connection: 〜たほうがいい／〜ばいい + んじゃない？／のではないでしょうか
examples: It's getting late. Maybe you should head home?
Wouldn't it be better to talk to the teacher first?

notes: After nouns and な-adjectives add 「な」: ✕「学生のではないか」→ ○「学生なのではないか」「静かなんじゃない？」.
With falling intonation and an exclamation mark, 「行くんじゃない！」 is a prohibition, “don't go!”, completely different from conjecture.
State the worry directly, as the bad thing that might happen, without an extra negative: ✕「落ちないのではないかと心配だ」 (this becomes worry that “I won't fail”) → ○「落ちるのではないかと心配だ」.
When advising a superior, 「〜たほうがいいんじゃないですか」 still sounds like instructing them; in business say 「〜てはいかがでしょうか」 or 「〜たほうがよろしいのではないでしょうか」.

daily.title: Guessing a friend's feelings
daily.description: A friend hasn't replied in a while, and you guess why with someone else.
daily.example: Maybe she's busy.

daily.title: Giving a friend advice
daily.description: A friend can't decide whether to see a doctor.
daily.example: Shouldn't you go to the hospital, just once?

daily.title: Worrying before going out
daily.description: You're afraid of being late, so you leave early.
daily.example: I thought the roads might be crowded, so I left early.

work.title: Giving an opinion in a meeting
work.description: Gently disagreeing with a proposal.
work.example: Isn't this schedule a little tight?

work.title: Papers and commentary
work.description: Gently putting forward a view in an academic paper.
work.example: It may be that this result is due to the survey method.

etymology: Made of explanatory 「の」 + negative 「ではない」 + question 「か」. Literally “isn't it the case that ...?”, it uses a rhetorical question to express a guess. In speech, 「の」 becomes 「ん」 and 「では」 becomes 「じゃ」, giving 「んじゃない」.

similar.title: 〜じゃない（か）(confirmation)
similar.explanation: Same source: both are built from 「ではない＋か」. 「〜じゃないか」 confirms known facts or expresses surprise; 「〜のではないか」 has 「の」 and expresses an uncertain conjecture.

similar.title: 〜のではないだろうか
similar.explanation: Same source and similar meaning: 「〜のではないだろうか」 replaces the part before 「か」 with the conjectural 「だろう」, which is even softer and more written, common in essays and commentary.

similar.title: 〜だろう
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜だろう」 is a fairly direct conjecture. 「〜のではないか」 uses a rhetorical question and does not assert directly, so it sounds softer and more objective.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜かもしれない」 just says “it's possible,” with low certainty and neutral. 「〜のではないか」 leans toward the speaker's own view and is often used to put forward an opinion gently.

formation: It consists of the explanatory 「の」 + the negative 「ではない」 + the question 「か」; literally, “isn't it the case that ...?” 「の」 organizes the content into “an explanation” and offers it, and the negative question hands the final judgment to the listener, so the speaker does not assert directly and forms a mild conjecture. Offering “a bad thing may happen” as a conjecture is worry; offering “this way is better” as a conjecture is a suggestion with no sense of command. In speech 「の」 becomes 「ん」 and 「では」 becomes 「じゃ」, producing 「〜んじゃない」.

meaning: Expresses a wish as if talking to yourself: “I wish ...”, “I hope ...”. Can also be a soft request.
connection: Verb ない-form + かな（あ）／かしら

senses.label: Hoping for ...
senses.meaning: Hoping something will happen, like “I wish ...” or “I hope ... soon”. Usually said to yourself, mostly about things you can't control.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + かな／かなあ; women also say 「〜ないかしら」. Common: 「早く〜ないかな」
examples: I can't wait for summer vacation.
I hope it's sunny tomorrow.
I wish someone could help me.

senses.label: Soft request
senses.meaning: 「〜てくれないかな」 gently asks someone to do something, like “Could you ...?”. Casual, for people you're close to.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれないかな／もらえないかな
examples: Could you hold this bag for me for a sec?
Could you lend me a little money?

notes: 「〜ないかな」 can also be a simple worry or question, “I wonder if it won't ...” (「彼、来ないかな」); use words like 「早く」 and the context to tell whether it is a wish.
「〜じゃないかな」 is a conjecture, “isn't it ...?”, not a wish: 「雨じゃないかな」 = it's probably rain.
「〜てくれないかな」 is only for close friends. To superiors or clients say 「〜ていただけないでしょうか」; otherwise it sounds casual and rude.
The wish use targets things you can't control. For things you decide yourself, change the phrasing: ✕「私が早く起きないかな」→ ○「早く起きられたらいいな」.

daily.title: Waiting for the bus
daily.description: The bus is late, and you mutter impatiently.
daily.example: I wish the bus would hurry up and come.

daily.title: Looking forward to the weekend
daily.description: Longing for the weekend on a weekday.
daily.example: I can't wait for the weekend.

daily.title: Asking family for help
daily.description: Asking a family member for help while cooking.

work.title: Muttering to a coworker
work.description: Working late and hoping it ends soon.
work.example: I wish this meeting would end soon.

etymology: Made of the negative 「ない」 + 「かな」 (asking yourself). Literally “I wonder if it won't ...”, this negative self-question expresses a wish that it will happen.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: Same source: both end in 「かな」. The affirmative 「〜かな」 is a self-question, “I wonder if ...” (「明日晴れるかな」); adding the negative, 「〜ないかな」, turns it into a hope, “I wish ...”.

similar.title: 〜といい・〜たらいい (hope)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜といい・〜たらいい」 also express hope (「明日晴れるといいな」) and state the wish directly. 「〜ないかな」 uses a self-question and sounds more like “I'm hoping, I can't wait.”

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜てほしい」 directly says you want someone to do something. 「〜てくれないかな」 is a mutter, more indirect, and doesn't sound like an order.

similar.title: 〜ないものか・〜ないものだろうか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning and structure: 「〜ないものか」 also expresses strong hope with “negative + question,” “can't it be ...?”, but is more literary and more urgent.

formation: It consists of the negative 「ない」 + the self-questioning final particle 「かな」 (the question 「か」 + the exclamatory 「な」); literally, “I wonder if it won't ...”. When you ask yourself a negative question, what the speaker hopes for is actually the affirmative (“it would be nice if it did”), so “isn't it going to ...?” becomes the wish “I hope it ....” This is the same idea as 「〜ないものか」, which expresses hope with a negative question. Add 「てくれる／もらえる」 and the wish is aimed at the other person's action, becoming a mild request voiced as a mutter.

meaning: Shows the standpoint or basis for a judgment: “from the viewpoint of ...”, “judging from ...”.
connection: Noun + から見ると／から見れば／から見て／からすると／からすれば

senses.label: From ...'s point of view
senses.meaning: Looks at something from a certain person's standpoint, like “in the eyes of ...” or “to ...”. The noun is usually a person or group.
senses.connection: Noun (person・standpoint) + から見ると／から見れば／から見たら／からすると
examples: To a child, the adult world is full of strange things.
To foreigners, Japanese customs may seem unusual.
To parents, their children are always children.

senses.label: Judging from ...
senses.meaning: Makes an inference based on something, like “judging from ...”. The second part is usually a guess with 「〜ようだ」, 「〜らしい」, or 「〜だろう」.
senses.connection: Noun (evidence) + から見ると／からすると／から見て
examples: From the looks of things, he seems to have gone home already.
Judging from the color of the sky, it will probably rain tomorrow.
Judging from these footprints, the culprit is probably a big man.

senses.label: No matter who looks
senses.meaning: 「誰から見ても」 and 「どこから見ても」 mean “anyone would see that ...” or “any way you look at it ...”.
senses.connection: Question word + から見ても
examples: Anyone would agree his work is wonderful.

notes: 「窓から見ると海が見える」 is the literal “looking from the window”; it does not mean “from the viewpoint of ...”. Context tells them apart.
It is followed by an opinion, judgment or conjecture, so it differs from 「にとって」: ✕「私にとって、彼は来ないと思う」→ ○「私から見ると、彼は来ないと思う」; 「にとって」 is usually followed by evaluations such as 「大切だ」「難しい」.
「〜から見ると」 stresses the viewpoint; for “judging from ...” 「〜からすると」 and 「〜から見て」 are more common: 「この様子からすると、もう帰ったようだ」.
With a person in sense 1, it expresses “that person's standpoint and feelings”, not the speaker's view: 「親からすれば、心配でたまらない」 means the parents are worried, not “I” am. Do not mix up the subject.
Being able to take a person is the biggest difference from 「〜からいうと」: ○「外国人からすると、敬語は難しい」 ✕「外国人からいうと、敬語は難しい」.

daily.title: Talking about the generation gap
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about how your values differ from your parents'.
daily.example: To our parents' generation, the way we work seems hard to understand.

daily.title: Guessing a friend's situation
daily.description: Seeing a friend's face and guessing what happened.
daily.example: Judging from your face, something good happened, right?

daily.title: Talking about parents
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about why parents worry so much.

work.title: Thinking from the customer's side
work.description: In a meeting, reminding everyone to see things from the customer's standpoint.
work.example: From the customer's point of view, I think this explanation is hard to understand.

work.title: Analyzing data
work.description: Making a judgment based on data.
work.example: Judging from the sales trend, further growth is expected next year.

etymology: Made of the particle 「から」 (from, a starting point) + the conditional forms of 「見る」 (to see) or 「する」. Literally “looking from ...”, the idea of a physical viewpoint extended to the standpoint or basis for a judgment.
formation: It consists of the case particle 「から」 (starting point) + 「見る」 (to look) + a conditional 「と／ば／たら」; literally, “if you look from ...”. 「から」 sets the first item as the observation point: if it is a person or position, “from the viewpoint of ...”; if it is evidence or signs, “judging from ...”. The conditional says “adopting this viewpoint, you reach the conclusion that follows,” so the second part is an opinion, judgment or conjecture, not a concrete action. 「からすると」 swaps 「見る」 for the more general 「する」, which weakens the visual tone and is used more for the basis of an inference.

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜にとって」 means “for ...” and is followed by an evaluation (「私にとって大切だ」). 「〜から見ると」 stresses “observing and judging from the viewpoint of ...” and can be followed by opinions and conjectures.

similar.title: 〜にしたら・〜にすれば
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜にしたら・〜にすれば」 means “putting yourself in ...'s position”; the first item must be a person and the clause usually guesses their feelings (「親にしたら心配だろう」). 「〜から見ると」 can also take evidence and signs.

similar.title: 〜からいうと・〜からいえば
similar.explanation: Same source: also built on 「から」. 「〜からいうと」 mostly takes abstract nouns such as 「立場」「経験」「点」, meaning “speaking from the standpoint of ...”, and doesn't take concrete people much.
